text: Tuesday night, under that bridge. Through Link, Jaeha looks out of Nib's eyes from a girder above the Kanghan enclosure.
Nib crouches on a flange barely wider than his feet, the black river far below.
On the rooftop, Jaeha reports with his eyes shut. Five people in work clothes, paid in cash.
The foreman's list has five numbers and no names. Nobody would ever ask where they went.
Bomi has already found the job, on an anonymous board.
Night work. F-rank summoners. Cash. No names. Next crew: Thursday, eleven p.m.
Below, the trucks load cores by the crate, faster since Saturday.
Then a guard swings his torch straight up at the girders.
Nib flattens against the steel, and a fat pigeon lands on his head. Pigeons, the guard grumbles.
Jaeha's mouth twitches. Nib says he hates pigeons.
Wednesday evening, the team crowds into the rooftop room, Borro's face filling the window.
Choi objects. Four days ago, Jaeha was on every screen in Korea. Everyone knows his face.
They know a face in an orange vest, Jaeha says. Under a respirator with a smoked visor, he's nobody.
And the biggest husk in Seoul walks in behind him?
No. Only Jaeha uses the front door. Nib takes the girders, Borro the riverbed, and Lyra swims in under the net, where the gate dips underwater.
Borro likes the river; it's quiet. And Lyra was swimming before this city had bridges.
And if something goes wrong? Choi waits outside with a rescue van, Bomi watches the fence, and Yerin has bandages.
Choi hates this plan. The van will be at the park gate from eleven.
Every night they wait, more cores go out, Jaeha argues. Choi cuts him off. He hates it. He didn't say no.
Seoa sits on her bed, staring at her knees, saying nothing.
Then she grabs his sleeve. Friday, seven o'clock, dinner. He comes home. Promise properly.
So he does, with a pinky promise and a thumb stamp.
From the windowsill, Nib looks out at the bridge lights.
Thursday, ten fifty p.m. Five people in grey coveralls wait by a van in a riverside park, Jaeha among them.
Foreman Gu hands out tabards and respirators, for the core dust. No names. You're your number.
Jaeha's tabard says four.
Number one is Uncle Pyo, a trap-tester since the very first gate. First night? Stay behind your husk and don't look down.
Ten years, he laughs, and his knees feel like thirty.
Number two, Dami, shows him her daughter on her lock screen. A few more nights of this, and she can buy her the good school bag.
And the Jang brothers, Woo and Ho, are saving for a chicken shop, if they can ever agree on its name.
Four years ago, that was Jaeha. Every one of them is him.
A whistle, and five faces vanish behind smoky visors.
Single file, they walk toward the glowing slit under pier seven, each behind a plain white husk.
Under the river, Borro walks the riverbed like a moving hill, and Lyra swims beside him toward the glow beneath the net.
Nib slides down a cable from the bridge and lands soundlessly on a container, right above a guard.
Jaeha steps into the light. Hyung. He's coming in.
Inside: a vast canyon in violet twilight, steel walkways bolted down its walls, and pipes as thick as trucks humming into the dark.
The crew stare at the drop. Uncle Pyo told them not to look down. Nobody ever listens.
Only Jaeha can see the three threads of light: Nib up in the pipes, Borro and Lyra in the river.
Husks first, says the foreman. Ten thousand won a trap.
A husk steps on a carved stone plate, and a stone spike smashes it into the abyss.
The foreman ticks his clipboard. One. Keep walking.
A window only Jaeha sees: unregistered gate, open four years and seventy-one days. Boss: alive.
Since the day Minseok didn't come out.
Along the ledge are old Far Side trap stones. Jaeha counts them. On every live one, the spiral opens left.
Pyo is about to step past his husk onto one. Jaeha whispers: husk first, and keep his left foot on the rivets.
His husk steps forward, and a stone blade cuts its legs off right where Pyo's knee would have been.
How did Four know that? Lucky guess, Uncle. It wasn't.
The foreman narrows his eyes at number four.
Down they go. A tiny cloaked figure keeps pace along the pipes; far below, two shapes move in the river.
Ho says the rail is throbbing, like something down there is breathing. It's the pipes, says Woo.
At the first landing stands an engineers' cabin, bolted to the rock.
And bad news for the foreman: the heir is coming down tonight, with an inspection order from the board.
He rounds on the crew with his stun baton crackling. When she comes, nobody talks. They're husks.
Who's the heir, Ho whispers. Somebody who never worked a night in her life, says Woo.
Then, from above: a sharp clack, in perfect rhythm.
Forty polished white husks march down two by two, every foot landing at once.
The crew flatten against the rock, and the foreman bows deep. Only number four stays put, watching the husks' feet.
A white heeled boot steps onto the steel.
The column parts, and down the middle walks a woman in white, baton in hand, as if the abyss isn't there.
She looks down the row like stock on a shelf. So these are the numbers her family pays in cash.
Kanghan's heir, Jaeha thinks. In the gate her family says doesn't exist.
She points her baton into the dark, and forty blank faces turn with it. Number four walks in front of her.
Behind his visor, Jaeha bows. Of course, ma'am. His husk is ready. It's a very brave husk.
Far below, a single throb of violet light runs down the pipes and fades.
